documentNotes.title: Instructions
documentNotes.statement:
*Entia non multiplicanda sunt praeter necessitatem*

**DO NOT OPEN THIS TEST UNTIL YOU ARE TOLD TO BEGIN**

1. **Please show all work, and do not hesitate to use explanatory words in addition to equations. Partial credit will be awarded**.

2. Begin each problem on a fresh sheet of paper. In the upper right-hand corner of each page, write your name, problem number, and the page number/total number of pages for this problem (e.g., "A2, 3/4" for "Problem A2, page 3 of four").

3. You may use a non-programmable calculator, but may not use any tables, books, notes, or collections of formulas.

4. Work Part A first. You have ninety minutes to complete all four problems.

5. After you have completed Part A, you may take a break.

6. Then work Part B. You have 90 minutes to complete both problems.

transcription.notes: Masthead: 'United States Physics Team', motto 'Entia non multiplicanda sunt praeter necessitatem', '1997 Exam 2' (the semifinal exam; catalogue round II agrees). Part A (A1-A4) and Part B (B1, B2) are problems 1-4 and 5-6; parts printed as '(a, 5)' are labelled '(a)' with the number as points. No problem totals or paper total are printed (parts sum to 20 per A problem, 40 per B problem); time limit 90 + 90 minutes. The problems PDF has a usable text layer (symbol fonts garbled); the solutions PDF has no text layer: A2 is a faded typed scan, all other solutions are handwritten scans transcribed as read, with printed per-line point values (2), (1), (4) kept in A2. Printed forms kept as printed: 'Avagadro’s number' (a name, not changed); A3(d) 'that it, what is the net work' (for 'that is'; a real word, kept); A4(a) 'by merely giving an qualitative argument' (article agreement error kept as printed per D-P28); B2(a) 'where ρ the atmosphere’s density' (missing 'is', kept); graph title 'Pressure vsTime' (inside the figure). The B1 figure labels the density n0 while the text writes n_o; the handwritten B1 solution labels the energy-density rewrite of (n_o)max as '(e)' on page 9 and the Ampère-law part also as '(e)' on page 10; both kept as written. In the handwritten A4(b) 'Alternate' box the result reads 'E = E_o(1-γ)' (as written; presumably E_o(1 - E_o/γ)). Page 10 of the solutions starts with a partly cut-off line read as 'Apply Amperes law,'. Handwritten solutions write 2mc² where the problem uses 2Mc²; kept as written.

problems.title: A1
problems.statement: A laser may be constructed from two main components: a resonant cavity of length $L$ formed from two highly reflecting flat mirrors, and a gas-filled tube that emits light when excited by a high voltage. Placed inside the otherwise evacuated cavity, the tube creates light which bounces back and forth between the mirrors such that standing light waves are produced within the cavity. (The radiation can be let out through a tiny window in one of the mirrors, but in this problem we are interested in what goes inside the cavity.)

figures.alt: Two vertical flat mirrors, each labelled Mirror, a distance L apart (arrow labelled L between them); between them a horizontal gas tube labelled ACME TUBES INC.

parts.label: (a)
parts.statement: What are the frequencies possible for the standing light waves in the cavity? Express your answer in terms of the cavity length $L$ and the speed of light in vacuum, $c$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.statement: Suppose the plasma tube emits light of a pure frequency $f_o = 5\times10^{14}$ Hz. Which standing wave mode (specified by an integer $n_o$) is excited in the cavity if $L = 1.5$ m?

parts.label: (c)
parts.statement: Suppose the plasma tube emits light not of a pure frequency, but emits light having all the frequencies in the range $f_o \pm \Delta f$, where $f_o = 5\times10^{14}$ Hz, and $\Delta f = 1\times10^{9}$ Hz. How many standing wave modes are excited in the cavity if $L = 1.5$ m?

parts.label: (d)
parts.statement: Using the $f_o$ and $\Delta f$ of part (c), what is the largest value of $L$ such that only *one* standing wave mode will be excited in the cavity, thereby giving the laser only *one* output frequency?

problems.statementAfterParts: (Adapted from A.P. French, *Vibrations and Waves*, Norton, NY, 1971).

solution.statement:
**(a)** The modes are

$$L = \frac{n\lambda}{2} \qquad \text{where } c = \lambda f$$

$$\Rightarrow\ f_n = \frac{nc}{2L} \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$$

**(b)**

$$n_o = \frac{2Lf_{n_o}}{c} = \frac{2(1.5\,\mathrm{m})(5\times10^{14}/\mathrm{s})}{3\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}} = 5\times10^{6}$$

**(c)**

$$f_{n_o} \pm \Delta f = (n_o \pm \Delta n)\frac{c}{2L}$$

$$\cancel{f_{n_o}} \pm \Delta f = \cancel{\frac{n_o c}{2L}} \pm \frac{c}{2L}\Delta n$$

$$\Delta n = \frac{2L}{c}\Delta f = \frac{2(1.5\,\mathrm{m})(1\times10^{9}/\mathrm{s})}{3\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}} = 10$$

So the frequencies being excited into resonance are those corresponding to

$$\underbrace{n_o,\ n_o \pm 1,\ n_o \pm 2,\ \ldots,\ n_o \pm 10}_{21\ \text{modes}}$$

**(d)** From (c), we note that as $L$ gets shorter, $\Delta n$ gets smaller ($\Delta f$ is fixed by the plasma tube, not the cavity). Decreasing $L$, the first modes to go away are $n_o \pm 10$, next is $n_o \pm 9$, etc. To lop off $\pm 10$ modes, the length $L$ must be $\frac{1}{10}$ as long as before (since $L \propto \Delta n$). Hence

$$L = \frac{1.5\,\mathrm{m}}{10} = 15\,\mathrm{cm}.$$

figures.alt: Hand sketch of the standing-wave modes between two walls a distance L apart: one loop for n = 1, two loops for n = 2, three loops for n = 3, then vertical dots.

problems.title: A2
problems.statement:
A ball is tossed onto the floor, where it makes a succession of bounces as illustrated in the figure below. Assume that because of internal elasticity and friction with the floor, at each bounce the magnitude of the vertical velocity component is reduced by a factor $\epsilon_y$ and the horizontal component is reduced by a factor $\epsilon_x$. That is, if $v_{oy,n+1}$ denotes the $y$-component of the velocity as the ball emerges from the $(n+1)$st bounce, then $v_{oy,n+1} = \epsilon_y v_{oy,n}$, and similarly for the $x$-component. Note that $\epsilon_y$ and $\epsilon_x$ are $< 1$. Thus after each bounce, the ball moves slower and hops a shorter distance than it did after the preceding bounce.

Let the ball's succession of bounces traverse a total horizontal distance $L^*$ which takes the time $t^*$. (As a practical matter, we measure $L^*$ and $t^*$ as the length and time where the bounces become imperceptible; mathematically, the number of bounces goes to infinity.) Find $\theta_1$, the angle the ball's velocity makes with the horizontal immediately after the first bounce, written in terms of $L^*$, $t^*$, $\epsilon_y$, $\epsilon_x$, and needed constants. Neglect air resistance.

figures.alt: A ball's trajectory arriving from the upper left and bouncing along a horizontal floor with ever smaller arcs; bounce points labelled 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (row label Bounce); angle θ1 marked between the floor and the dotted tangent after bounce 1; dotted verticals mark the hop intervals L1, t1 and L2, t2, and the whole distance L*, t* from bounce 1 to where the bounces die out.

solution.statement:
Each hop is a projectile motion, so that

$$x = v_{ox}t, \qquad (2)$$

and

$$t = 2v_{oy}/g \quad (\text{from } 0 = y = v_{oy}t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2). \qquad (2)$$

and upon eliminating $t$, the range $L$ of a hop is

$$L = 2v_{ox}v_{oy}/g. \qquad (2)$$

Since $v_{oy,n+1} = \epsilon_y v_{oy,n}$ and $v_{ox,n+1} = \epsilon_x v_{ox,n}$, it follows that

$$v_{oy,n+1} = \epsilon_y^{\,n} v_{oy,1} \qquad (1)$$

$$v_{ox,n+1} = \epsilon_x^{\,n} v_{ox,1} \qquad (1)$$

$$L_{n+1} = (\epsilon_y\epsilon_x)^n L_1 \qquad (2)$$

$$t_{n+1} = L_{n+1}/v_{ox,n+1} = \epsilon_y^{\,n} t_1 \qquad (2)$$

The total range is

$$\begin{aligned} L^* &= L_1 + L_2 + L_3 + L_4 + \ldots \\ &= L_1[1 + \epsilon_y\epsilon_x + (\epsilon_y\epsilon_x)^2 + (\epsilon_y\epsilon_x)^3 + \ldots] \\ &= L_1[1 - \epsilon_y\epsilon_x]^{-1} \qquad (2) \end{aligned}$$

The total time is

$$\begin{aligned} t^* &= t_1 + t_2 + t_3 + t_4 + \ldots \\ &= t_1[1 + \epsilon_y + (\epsilon_y)^2 + (\epsilon_y)^3 + \ldots] \\ &= t_1[1 - \epsilon_y]^{-1} \qquad (2) \end{aligned}$$

The angle $\theta_1$ is given by

$$\begin{aligned} \theta_1 &= \tan^{-1}(v_{oy,1}/v_{ox,1}) \\ &= \tan^{-1}(g t_1^2/2L_1) \\ &= \tan^{-1}\{[g t^{*2}(1 - \epsilon_y)^2]/[2L^*(1 - \epsilon_y\epsilon_x)]\} \qquad (4) \end{aligned}$$

problems.title: A3
problems.statement:
The circuit shown consists of:

a 10 volt battery,\
a 1.0 µF capacitor,\
a 4.0 µF capacitor,\
a 50 Ω resistor,\
three 25 Ω resistors, and four switches, labeled $S_o$, $S_1$, $S_2$, $S_3$. All switches are initially open. In all cases assume that the circuit is completely insulated from its surroundings.

figures.alt: Circuit: a top rail feeds three vertical branches through resistors 25Ω, 25Ω and 50Ω; the first branch contains the 4.0 µF capacitor and switch S2, the second the 1.0 µF capacitor and switch S1, the third the 10 V battery and switch S0; a fourth branch on the left with a 25Ω resistor and switch S3 connects the node between the first 25Ω resistor and the 4.0 µF capacitor to the bottom rail.

parts.label: (a)
parts.statement: Switches $S_o$, $S_1$, $S_2$ are closed. Switch $S_3$ remains open. After a very long time, what is the charge on each capacitor?

answer.value: q1 = 10 µC on the 1.0 µF capacitor; q2 = 40 µC on the 4.0 µF capacitor

parts.label: (b)
parts.statement: Switch $S_3$ is also closed, so that all four switches are closed. After a very long time, what is the charge on each capacitor?

answer.value: q2 = 10 µC on the 4.0 µF capacitor; q1 = 5 µC on the 1.0 µF capacitor

parts.label: (c)
parts.statement: Switches $S_o$ and $S_3$ are opened simultaneously. Switches $S_1$ and $S_2$ are left closed. After a very long time, what is the charge on each capacitor?

answer.value: q2 = 12 µC on the 4.0 µF capacitor; q1 = 3 µC on the 1.0 µF capacitor

parts.label: (d)
parts.statement: Switches $S_2$ and $S_3$ are opened. Switches $S_o$ and $S_1$ are closed. After a very long time has passed you insert into the 1.0 µF capacitor a slab of dielectric material. After the dielectric is inserted, it totally fills the region between the plates. The material's dielectric constant is 3.0. What is the total work done in inserting the dielectric (that it, what is the net work done by you *and* the battery)?

solution.statement:
**(a)** as $t \to \infty$ the circuit becomes:

In parallel, so

$$V_1 = V_2 = V_o = 10\,\mathrm{V}$$

$$\Rightarrow\ q_1 = C_1V_o = (1\,\mu\mathrm{F})(10\,\mathrm{V}) = 10\,\mu\mathrm{C}$$

$$q_2 = C_2V_o = (4\,\mu\mathrm{F})(10\,\mathrm{V}) = 40\,\mu\mathrm{C}$$

**(b)** as $t \to \infty$, current flows through outer loop only,

$$I = \frac{10\,\mathrm{V}}{100\,\Omega} = \frac{1}{10}\,\mathrm{A}$$

$C_2$ is in parallel with the $25\,\Omega$ resistor by $S_3$:

$$V = IR = (\tfrac{1}{10}\,\mathrm{A})(25\,\Omega) = 2.5\,\mathrm{V}$$

$$\Rightarrow\ q_2 = C_2V_2 = (4\,\mu\mathrm{F})(2.5\,\mathrm{V}) = 10\,\mu\mathrm{C}$$

$C_1$ is in parallel with $50\,\Omega$

$$V = (\tfrac{1}{10}\,\mathrm{A})(50\,\Omega) = 5\,\mathrm{V}$$

$$q_1 = C_1V_1 = (1\,\mu\mathrm{F})(5\,\mathrm{V}) = 5\,\mu\mathrm{C}$$

**(c)** From (b), $q_{total} = q_1 + q_2 = 15\,\mu\mathrm{C}$

Now the charge may only redistribute itself until $V_1 = V_2$

$$q_1 + q_2 = 15\,\mu\mathrm{C} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{q_1}{C_1} = \frac{q_2}{C_2}$$

$$q_1 = \frac{C_1}{C_2}q_2 = \frac{1}{4}q_2$$

$$\Rightarrow\ \frac{5}{4}q_2 = 15\,\mu\mathrm{C} \quad \text{or} \quad q_2 = 12\,\mu\mathrm{C} \quad \Rightarrow\ q_1 = 3\,\mu\mathrm{C}$$

**(d)** *initial*: $C = 1\,\mu\mathrm{F}$, $V_o = 10\,\mathrm{V}$; $q_i = (1\,\mu\mathrm{F})(10\,\mathrm{V}) = 10\,\mu\mathrm{C}$

*final*: $C = 3\,\mu\mathrm{F}$, $V_o = 10\,\mathrm{V}$; $q_f = (3\,\mu\mathrm{F})(10\,\mathrm{V}) = 30\,\mu\mathrm{C}$

Battery connected, $V$ does not change, but $q$ does

$$\text{Work} = \Delta(\text{Energy})$$

$$\begin{aligned} W_{Battery} + W_{you} &= \Delta(\tfrac{1}{2}CV^2) \\ &= \tfrac{1}{2}(3C_1 - C_1)V^2 \\ &= \tfrac{1}{2}(2\,\mu\mathrm{F})(10\,\mathrm{V})^2 \\ &= 100\,\mu\mathrm{J} \end{aligned}$$

figures.alt: Hand sketch for (a): capacitors C2 and C1 and the battery V0 connected in parallel.
Hand sketch for (b): a single loop with a 100Ω resistor and a 10 V battery.
Hand sketch for (b): current 1/10 A through the 25Ω resistor and closed switch S3, with capacitor C2 across them; a cloud note reads V = IR = (1/10 A)(25Ω) = 2.5 V.
Hand sketch for (b): two 25Ω resistors in series with switch S3, capacitor C1 across them; a cloud note reads V = (1/10 A)(50Ω) = 5 V.
Hand sketch for (c): capacitors C2 = 4 µF and C1 = 1 µF connected in parallel.
Hand sketch for (d), initial: capacitor C = 1 µF connected to the battery V0 = 10 V.
Hand sketch for (d), final: capacitor C = 3 µF filled with hatched dielectric, connected to the battery V0 = 10 V.

problems.title: A4
problems.statement: An atom in an excited state typically decays by emitting a photon. The atom is originally in some excited state $S'$, and after the decay it is in the ground state $S$. We usually think of the photon as carrying away the energy difference between states $S'$ and $S$. In this problem we examine this process closely.

parts.label: (a)
parts.statement: Consider a stationary, isolated atom in some excited state $S'$. Before decay the mass of the atom is $M'$. The atom decays into the ground state $S$. In the ground state the mass of the atom is $M$. Thus the energy $(M'-M)c^2$, which we denote here as $E_o$, is the energy that is released by the atom, and is therefore an upper limit on the energy that the photon could possibly carry away ($c$ is the speed of light). Let $E$ denote the energy of the outgoing photon. Without solving any equation, by merely giving an qualitative argument, explain why $E$ must be strictly less than $E_o$ in the case of an isolated excited atom undergoing radiative decay.

answer.value: To conserve momentum the atom must recoil, so it carries some kinetic energy K, leaving less than Eo for the photon.

parts.label: (b)
parts.statement:
Quantify your answer to part (a) by showing that, approximately,

$E \approx E_o\,[\,1 - (\,E_o / 2Mc^2\,)\,]$, where $E_o / 2Mc^2 \ll 1$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.statement: Consider an atom decaying from the excited state $S'$ to the ground state $S$, where $Mc^2 = 2\times10^{11}$ eV and $E_o = 4\times10^{5}$ eV. A photon energy corresponds to a radiation frequency. Thus the energy difference $E_o - E$ corresponds to a frequency shift $\Delta f = f_o - f$. Calculate the fractional frequency shift $\Delta f / f_o$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.statement: Another way to produce a frequency shift is the Doppler effect, produced by relative motion between source and observer. The atom of part (c) emits the photon energy $E$, which corresponds to light frequency $f$. With what speed and in what direction would an observer have to move relative to this photon, to Doppler-shift its frequency back to the value $f_o$ corresponding to the energy $E_o$? The observer’s speed $v$ is $\ll c$.

answer.note: The observer must move towards the photon.

solution.statement:
**(a)** To conserve momentum the atom must recoil. Thus after emitting the photon, the atom carries some kinetic energy $K$, leaving *less* than $E_o$ for photon.

**(b)** Before decay: $(\text{Energy, momentum}) = (M'c^2, 0)$. After decay: atom $(Mc^2 + K, -p)$, photon $(E, E/c)$.

*Conservation of Energy*

$$M'c^2 = Mc^2 + K + E$$

$$(M' - M)c^2 = K + E$$

$$E_o = K + E$$

*Cons. of Momentum*

$$0 = \frac{E}{c} - p$$

$$p = \frac{E}{c}$$

[since the atom is heavy, $v \ll c$ and $K = p^2/2m$, or $p \approx \sqrt{2mK}$ for *atom*]

$$\therefore\ \sqrt{2mK} = \frac{E}{c} \ \Rightarrow\ K = \frac{E^2}{2mc^2}$$

$\{$ or, relativistically,

$$(Mc^2)^2 = (K + Mc^2)^2 - (pc)^2$$

$$\Rightarrow\ K = Mc^2\left[\sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{E}{Mc^2}\right)^2} - 1\right] \approx E^2/2mc^2 \ \}$$

[given $\dfrac{E_o}{2mc^2} \ll 1$ since $K$ and $E$ are $< E_o$, $\dfrac{K}{2mc^2}$ and $\dfrac{E}{2mc^2}$ are $\ll 1$ too]

Conservation of Energy Equation becomes

$$E_o = \frac{E^2}{2mc^2} + E$$

$$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow\ E &= E_o\left(1 + \frac{E}{2mc^2}\right)^{-1} \\ &\approx E_o\left(1 - \frac{E}{2mc^2}\right) \qquad \text{Iterate} \\ &\approx E_o\left[1 - \frac{E_o(1 - E/2mc^2)}{2mc^2}\right] \end{aligned}$$

[Alternate: Quadratic formula —

$$E^2 + \gamma E + \gamma E_o = 0 \quad \text{where } \gamma = 2mc^2$$

$$\Rightarrow\ E = \frac{\gamma}{2}\left[-1 \pm \left(1 + \frac{4E_o}{\gamma}\right)^{1/2}\right] \approx \frac{\gamma}{2}\left[-1 \pm \left(1 + \frac{2E_o}{\gamma} - \frac{2E_o^2}{\gamma^2}\right)\right]$$

since $E > 0$ take $+$

$$E = E_o(1 - \gamma)$$

Note: 2nd order needed in Binomial]

If $\delta \equiv \dfrac{E_o}{2mc^2} \ll 1$ then $\dfrac{EE_o}{(2mc^2)^2} \approx \delta^2$ is negligible

$$\Rightarrow\ \boxed{E \approx E_o\left(1 - \frac{E_o}{2mc^2}\right)}$$

**(c)** From part (b),

$$E_o - E = \frac{E_o^2}{2mc^2}$$

Using $E = hf$, and writing $E_o^2 = hf_oE_o$,

$$h(f_o - f) = \frac{hf_oE_o}{2mc^2}$$

$$\frac{\Delta f}{f_o} = \frac{E_o}{2mc^2} = \frac{4\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{eV}}{2(2\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{eV})} = 10^{-6}$$

**(d)** For $v \ll c$, Doppler shift says

$$\frac{v}{c} \approx \frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} \qquad \text{where } c = \lambda f$$

Since $f_o > f$, the observer must move towards the photon

$$\Delta\lambda = c\,\Delta\!\left(\frac{1}{f}\right) \approx -\frac{\Delta f}{f^2}\,c$$

[Alternate: $c = \lambda f$; $dc = 0 = \lambda\,df + f\,d\lambda$; $d\lambda = -\lambda\dfrac{df}{f}$; $\dfrac{d\lambda}{\lambda} = -\dfrac{df}{f}$; minus sign means that a *decrease* in $\lambda$ corresponds to *increase* in frequency!]

$\therefore$ (in magnitude)

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{v}{c} &\approx \frac{\Delta f}{f^2}\,\frac{c}{\lambda} \\ &= \frac{\Delta f}{f} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} v &= \frac{\Delta f}{f_o}\,c \\ &= 10^{-6}\,c \qquad \left(\text{using } \frac{\Delta f}{f_o} = 10^{-6} \text{ from part (c)}\right) \\ &= 300\,\mathrm{m/s} \end{aligned}$$

figures.alt: Hand sketch for (b): before decay a circle labelled M' at rest; after decay a circle labelled M moving left with momentum p and a photon dot moving right, labelled photon.
Hand sketch for (d): a photon dot moving right with speed c and a stick-figure observer moving left towards it with speed v.

problems.title: B1
problems.statement: Consider an infinitely long, cylindrical cloud of electrons. The cloud has radius $R$, the number density of electrons has the uniform value $n_o$, the charge of each electron is $-e$ (where $e > 0$), and the mass of each electron is $m$. The cloud is surrounded by vacuum. There is a constant, uniform magnetic field along the cylinder's axis (the $z$-axis), so that $\mathbf{B} = B_o\mathbf{k}$, with $B_o > 0$. The cloud of electrons is rotating about the $z$-axis with angular velocity $\omega$ as shown in the figure. The speeds are non-relativistic. [A gas of charged particles is called a "plasma."]

figures.alt: An upright cylinder of radius R (radius arrow drawn on the top face) with dotted continuations above and below; the vertical Z-axis with a curved arrow marking the rotation ω; n0 written inside the cylinder.

parts.label: (a)
parts.statement: Find the electric field at the radius $r < R$ within the cloud.

parts.label: (b)
parts.statement: Find the total force on an electron located at the radius $r$ within the cloud, neglecting any magnetic field induced by the cloud's rotation. (This neglect will be justified in part (f) below.)

parts.label: (c)
parts.statement: Using Newton's second law, show that there are two values of $\omega$ possible for the electrons to steadily orbit the cylinder's axis. Write these values of $\omega$ in terms of two other frequencies relevant to such problems: the cyclotron frequency $\omega_c = eB_o/m$, and the "plasma frequency" $\omega_p = [\,n_oe^2 / \epsilon_o m\,]^{1/2}$, where $\epsilon_o$ is the permittivity of empty space.

parts.label: (d)
parts.statement: Find the largest electron number density $(n_o)_{max}$ that can be confined by the applied magnetic field $B_o\mathbf{k}$. Write your answer in terms of the magnetic field energy density $B^2/2\mu_o$ and the electron's mass energy $mc^2$.
parts.statementAfter: [This theoretical limit is called the *Brillouin limit*, and plays a key role in the confinement of plasmas consisting of particles all of like charge.]

parts.label: (e)
parts.statement: At a point located at radius $r$ within the cylindrical cloud, calculate the magnetic field induced by the cloud's rotation. Assume that the field induced on the axis of symmetry is zero.

parts.label: (f)
parts.statement: Determine the force on a charge in the cloud, due to the induced magnetic field of part (e). Show that the magnitude of this force divided by the magnitude of the electric force is $v^2/c^2$, where $v$ is the speed of the charge and $c$ is the speed of light. [This shows that the effect of the induced field is ignorable when the rotation speeds are non-relativistic.]

solution.statement:
**(a)** Use Gauss' law:

$$\text{flux of } \vec{E} = \frac{1}{\epsilon_o}(\text{charge enclosed})$$

$$E\,2\pi rh = \frac{1}{\epsilon_o}(n_oe)(\pi r^2h)$$

$$E = \left(\frac{n_oe}{2\epsilon_o}\right)r$$

$$\vec{E} = \frac{n_oe}{2\epsilon_o}\,r\,(-\hat{r}) \qquad \text{radially } \underline{\text{in}}$$

[gaussian surface: cylinder, $r \le R$, height $h$; no flux through end caps ($\vec{E}\cdot\hat{n} = 0$ there)]

**(b)**

$$\begin{aligned} \vec{F} &= q(\vec{E} + \vec{v}\times\vec{B}) \\ &= -e\left[-\frac{n_oer}{2\epsilon_o}\hat{r} + r\omega B_o\hat{r}\right] \end{aligned}$$

[$\vec{B} = B_o\hat{k}$, $\vec{v} = r\omega\hat{\theta}$, $\hat{\theta}\times\hat{k} = \hat{r}$]

$$\vec{F} = \left(\frac{n_oe^2r}{2\epsilon_o} - r\omega B_oe\right)\hat{r}$$

**(c)**

$$\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$$

$$\left(\frac{n_oe^2r}{2\epsilon_o} - r\omega B_oe\right)\hat{r} = m\frac{(r\omega)^2}{r}(-\hat{r})$$

$$\Rightarrow\ \frac{n_oe^2}{2\epsilon_o} - \omega B_oe + m\omega^2 = 0$$

$$\omega^2 - \left(\frac{Be}{m}\right)\omega + \frac{n_oe^2}{2\epsilon_om} = 0$$

$$\omega^2 - \omega_c\omega + \tfrac{1}{2}\omega_p^2 = 0$$

[$\omega_c \equiv \dfrac{B_oe}{m}$, $\omega_p^2 \equiv \dfrac{n_oe^2}{\epsilon_om}$]

$$\omega = \frac{\omega_c}{2} \pm \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\omega_c^2 - 2\omega_p^2}$$

$$\omega = \frac{\omega_c}{2}\left(1 \pm \sqrt{1 - 2\left(\frac{\omega_p}{\omega_c}\right)^2}\right)$$

**(d)** Since $\omega$ is real, this requires

$$1 - 2\left(\frac{\omega_p}{\omega_c}\right)^2 \ge 0$$

$$\omega_p^2 \le \frac{1}{2}\omega_c^2$$

$$\frac{n_oe^2}{\epsilon_om} \le \frac{1}{2}\frac{e^2B_o^2}{m^2}$$

$$n_o \le \frac{B_o^2\epsilon_o}{2m} \qquad \text{so} \qquad (n_o)_{max} = \frac{B_o^2\epsilon_o}{2m}$$

**(e)**

$$(n_o)_{max} = \frac{B_o^2\epsilon_o}{2m} \qquad \text{use } \mu_o\epsilon_o = \frac{1}{c^2}$$

$$= \frac{B_o^2}{2m(\mu_oc^2)}$$

$$= \frac{B_o^2/2\mu_o}{mc^2} = \frac{\text{magnetic field energy density}}{\text{electron mass energy}}$$

**(e)** Apply Ampere's law,

$$\oint_C \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_oI_S \qquad \text{where } C = \text{boundary of } S$$

$$B'h = \mu_o\int_S j\,da$$

where

$$\begin{aligned} j &= \text{current density} \\ &= (n_oe)v \\ &= n_oer'\omega \end{aligned}$$

(or $\Sigma\, r\Delta r$)

$$B'h = \mu_o(n_oe\omega)\int_0^r r'(dr'\,h)$$

$$B'h = \mu_on_oe\omega h\int_0^r r'\,dr'$$

$$B' = \mu_on_oe\omega\frac{r^2}{2}$$

[$\vec{B}'$ = induced field $= B'\hat{k}$; given $\vec{B}' = 0$ on axis; note $\vec{B}'\cdot d\vec{l} = 0$ horizontally]

**(f)** Force due to induced magnetic field is $\vec{F}'$ where

$$\begin{aligned} \vec{F}' &= -e\,\vec{v}\times\vec{B}' = -e(r\omega\hat{\theta})\times\left(\mu_on_oe\omega\frac{r^2}{2}\hat{k}\right) \\ &= \frac{\mu_on_oe^2\omega^2r^3}{2}(-\hat{r}) \end{aligned}$$

[$\hat{\theta}\times\hat{k} = \hat{r}$; $v = r\omega$]

$$|\vec{F}'| = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_on_oe^2v^2r$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{|\vec{F}'|}{|\vec{F}_{el.}|} = \frac{\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_on_oe^2v^2r}{\tfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{n_oe^2r}{\epsilon_o}} = \mu_o\epsilon_ov^2 = \frac{v^2}{c^2}$$

(the denominator is $|e\vec{E}|$ where $|\vec{E}|$ is from part (a))

Hand sketch for (e): the rotating cylinder (rotation ω about the axis) with a rectangular Amperian loop C bounding surface S in a plane through the axis, height h, from radius r to outside; a hatched strip da = h dr at radius r' of width dr; current density j circulating; induced field B' upward; notes: B' = induced field = B' k; given B' = 0 on axis; note B'·dl = 0 horizontally.

problems.title: B2
problems.statement: An unmanned space probe approaches the surface of a planet whose atmosphere is pure CO$_2$ (molecular weight $M = 44$ gm/mol). Upon entering atmosphere, the probe descends straight down at a constant speed $v_o$, recording information about the atmospheric pressure, which is shown on the attached graph. Unfortunately, a technician forgot to calibrate the pressure-measuring instrument, so that the $P$-axis on the pressure vs. time graph has no units! (The technician has been reprimanded, but fortunately, as leader of the data analysis team, you have figured out how to use the data anyway.) Upon reaching the planet’s surface, the probe reports the surface temperature to be 400 K, and the gravitational field there to be 9.9 N/kg. The radius of the planet is $5.0\times10^{6}$ m. Model the atmosphere locally as an ideal gas.

figures.alt: Graph titled Pressure vsTime Data From Probe: vertical axis P(arbitrary units) from 0 to 60 with gridlines every 10, horizontal axis t(sec) with gridlines every 500 s, labelled 500, 1500, 2500, 3500; the curve rises from 0 at t = 0, slowly at first, passes about 10 near 1550 s, 30 near 3000 s, reaches 60 at about 4000 s and stays flat at 60 afterwards.

parts.label: (a)
parts.statement: Apply Newton’s Second Law to a small slab of the atmosphere of thickness $\Delta y$ that is in static equilibrium, to show that the change in pressure $\Delta P$ between the top and bottom sides of the slab is given by $\Delta P = \pm\rho g\Delta y$, where $\rho$ the atmosphere’s density and $g$ is the local gravitational field (the plus or minus sign is determined by the choice for the positive direction of the vertical $y$-axis; work out the sign in terms of your choice).

parts.label: (b)
parts.statement: Estimate the velocity $v_o$ with which the probe descends to the surface.

parts.label: (c)
parts.statement: Estimate the temperature of the atmosphere 15 km above the surface. Neglect the variation of the planet’s gravitational field between the surface and this height.

parts.label: (d)
parts.statement: Justify the neglect of the variation of the planet’s gravitational field between the surface and 15 km above the surface. Suggestion: Calculate the fractional difference between the gravitational field’s magnitude on the surface and its value 15 km above the surface, and assess whether that difference is significant compared to the accuracy of the estimate made in part (c).

answer.note: Δg/go = 2h/R = 6×10⁻³, much smaller than the accuracy of the estimate in part (c).

solution.statement:
**(a)** Apply $F = ma$ to a slab of atmosphere of thickness $\Delta y$, cross-sectional area $A$, density $\rho$. Take $y$ positive upwards.

Forces: $P(y+\Delta y)A$ (down), $P(y)A$ (up), $mg$ (down).

$$F = ma \quad (\text{which} = 0)$$

$$P(y)A - P(y+\Delta y)A - (\rho A\Delta y)g = 0$$

$$\underbrace{P(y+\Delta y) - P(y)}_{\Delta P} = -\rho g\Delta y$$

$$\Delta P = -\rho g\Delta y$$

[note $\rho = \rho(y)$, $g = g(y)$]

**(b)** Since $v_o = \dfrac{-\Delta y}{\Delta t}$ (probe going down, $y$ points up)

$\Delta P = -\rho g\Delta y$ gives

$$\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta t} = \rho g v_o \qquad \ldots(1)$$

Need $\rho$: From ideal gas eq. of state $PV = nRT$,

$$P = \frac{n}{V}RT \qquad \text{where } \frac{n}{V} = \frac{\#\,\text{moles}}{\text{vol.}} = \frac{\#\,\text{moles}}{\text{mass}}\,\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{vol.}}$$

$$\frac{n}{V} = \frac{1}{M}\rho$$

$$\Rightarrow\ P = \frac{\rho}{M}RT$$

$$\rho = \frac{PM}{RT} \qquad \ldots(2)$$

Using $\rho$ from (2) in (1),

$$\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta t} = \frac{PM}{RT}\,g v_o$$

$$v_o = \left(\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta t}\right)\frac{RT}{PMg} \qquad \ldots(3)$$

From graph, probe lands on surface at $t = 4000$ s

$$P = 60\ \text{units}, \quad g = 9.9\ \mathrm{N/kg}, \quad T = 400\ \mathrm{K}$$

[From graph: at surface

$$\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta t} = \frac{(60 - 55)\ \text{units}}{(4000 - 3900)\ \mathrm{s}} = .05\ \text{units/s}$$

[line from (3900, 55) to (4000, 60) is straight]]

From Eq. (3),

$$v_o = \frac{(.05\ \text{units/s})(8.3\ \mathrm{J/K\text{-}mol})(400\ \mathrm{K})}{(60\ \text{units})(44\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg/mol})(9.9\ \mathrm{N/kg})} \cong 6.4\ \mathrm{m/s}$$

**(c)** Probe was 15 km above surface

$$\Delta t = \frac{15\ \mathrm{km}}{6.4\ \mathrm{m/s}} \cong 2344\ \mathrm{s} \text{ before touchdown; ie., at}$$

$$t = (4000 - 2344)\ \mathrm{s} = 1656\ \mathrm{s}$$

at $t \approx 1650$ s, $P = 11$ units

slope at $t = 1650$ s is about the same as slope of line from (1500 s, 9 units) to (2000 s, 15 units)

$$\text{slope} \cong \frac{(15 - 9)\ \text{units}}{(2000 - 1500)\ \mathrm{s}} = .012\ \text{units/s}$$

$\approx .01$ to two sig. figures (like slope found above)

From Eq. (3),

$$T = \frac{PMg v_o}{R\left(\dfrac{\Delta P}{\Delta t}\right)}$$

$$\Rightarrow\ \frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{P_2}{P_1}\,\frac{(\Delta P/\Delta t)_1}{(\Delta P/\Delta t)_2} \qquad \begin{matrix}\text{Point 1: surface} \\ \text{Point 2: 15 km above surface}\end{matrix}$$

$$T_2 = \frac{11}{60}\left(\frac{.05}{.01}\right)400\ \mathrm{K} \cong 367\ \mathrm{K}$$

**(d)**

$$\begin{aligned} g(h) &= \frac{GM}{(R+h)^2} \\ &= \frac{GM}{R^2}\left(1 + \frac{h}{R}\right)^{-2} \\ &\cong g_o\left(1 - \frac{2h}{R}\right) \\ &\equiv g_o - \Delta g \end{aligned}$$

$$g_o = \frac{GM}{R^2}$$

where

$$\Delta g = \frac{2h}{R}g_o$$

$$\frac{\Delta g}{g_o} = \frac{2h}{R} = \frac{2(15\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m})}{5\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}} = 6\times10^{-3}$$

In part (c), the estimate of $P$ and $\Delta P/\Delta t$ at 15 km above the surface was much cruder than 6 parts out of a thousand.

Hand sketch for (a), geometry: a slab of area A and thickness Δy at height y above the ground, with a stick figure standing on the ground.
